```{r setup}
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
  library(scales); library(knitr); library(kableExtra); library(tidymodels)
  library(forcats); library(stringr); library(readr); library(tibble)
})
source("R/data_prep.R")
source("R/models.R")

theme_set(
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
          plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 2, 2))
)

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

housing <- prepare_housing_data()
d       <- housing$modelled
reg     <- get_model_results(d, "regression")
clf     <- get_model_results(d, "classification")

m_reg  <- reg$metrics |> select(model, .metric, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean)
se_reg <- reg$metrics |> select(model, .metric, std_err) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = std_err)
m_clf  <- clf$metrics |> select(model, .metric, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean)
se_clf <- clf$metrics |> select(model, .metric, std_err) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = std_err)

get_reg <- function(model, metric) {
  if (metric %in% names(m_reg)) return(m_reg[[metric]][m_reg$model == model])
  se_reg[[metric]][se_reg$model == model]
}
get_clf <- function(model, metric) {
  if (metric %in% names(m_clf)) return(m_clf[[metric]][m_clf$model == model])
  se_clf[[metric]][se_clf$model == model]
}

term_lab <- c(
  log_pop        = "log population",
  log_inc        = "log median household income",
  log_hv         = "log median home value",
  log_dens       = "log population density",
  owner_share    = "owner-occupied share",
  mf_stock_share = "multifamily share of stock",
  med_year_built = "median year built"
)

n_towns   <- nrow(d)
n_zero    <- sum(d$permits_per_1000 == 0)
n_permits <- sum(d$perm_total)
```

# Introduction

Maine has a housing shortage, and the state has only recently started requiring
towns to report their building permits every year. That makes permits the earliest
hard number we have on where new housing is actually being built. Our question is a
narrow one: which municipal characteristics go with a higher rate of new
construction?

We did not start there. The first target we tried was the total number of permits a
town issues, and it turned out to be a disappointing one. Permit counts track
population almost mechanically, so a model of counts mostly recovers how big a town
is, which we already knew from the population column. We switched to the permit
rate, permits issued per 1,000 residents, and kept the same candidate predictors:
median household income, median home value, population density, the owner-occupied
share, the multifamily share of the housing stock, and the median year the stock was
built.

The short version of what we found is that home value matters a great deal, income
does not, and density runs the opposite way from what we expected. On top of
population, the characteristics roughly double the share of variance explained,
reaching an R-squared of about 0.25 out of fold, and none of the flexible models we
tried buys anything over a plain linear model. A smaller second task puts a
different question to the same towns: which of them permitted any multifamily
housing at all?

# Dataset

Permit counts come from the 2025 Statewide Housing Data workbook, which combines a
municipal survey, records from the Land Use Planning Commission, and Census Building
Permits Survey estimates for the 220 municipalities that did not respond to the
survey. The characteristics come from the 2020-2024 American Community Survey
five-year estimates at the county subdivision level, joined to the Census Gazetteer
for land area. We matched 528 of the 529 workbook municipalities to an ACS
subdivision; the exception is the aggregate UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES row, which is not
a single place.

Table 1 lists the variables we use.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vars
#| tbl-cap: "Variables used in the analysis."
vars <- tribble(
  ~Variable, ~Source, ~Definition,
  "Permit rate", "workbook", "Permits issued in 2024 per 1,000 residents",
  "log population", "ACS B01003", "Total population (log)",
  "log income", "ACS B19013", "Median household income, dollars (log)",
  "log home value", "ACS B25077", "Median value of owner-occupied units, dollars (log)",
  "log density", "ACS + Gazetteer", "Residents per square mile of land (log)",
  "Owner share", "ACS B25003", "Share of occupied units that are owner-occupied",
  "Multifamily share", "ACS B25024", "Share of housing units in buildings with 2+ units",
  "Median year built", "ACS B25035", "Median year the housing stock was built"
)
kable(vars, booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, align = "lll", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(3, width = "7.0cm")
```

Two features of the permits are worth spelling out, because they shape everything
after this. First, a town reports through one of two channels, a local survey or
Census estimates, and the two do not agree exactly. Across the 169 towns that appear
in both, the local totals run about 8% above the Census estimate, so we keep the
reporting channel as a predictor rather than pretending the two series are
interchangeable. Second, the missingness is structural rather than random. Accessory
dwelling units and affordable-unit counts exist only for the 182 towns that filled
in the survey, the Census columns exist wherever the Census publishes them, and 90
municipalities report nothing at all. Dropping the non-reporting towns and one
unorganized-territory row with no population leaves 438 towns with a permit count,
and 419 of those also have the ACS characteristics. That 419 is the sample used
below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dist
#| fig-cap: "Permit rates across the 419 towns. (a) Permits per 1,000 residents, x-axis truncated at 40 (15% of towns are at zero). (b) Median rate by home-value quintile. (c) Median rate by density quintile."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 1.95
p_a <- d |>
  ggplot(aes(x = permits_per_1000)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, boundary = 0, fill = "grey35", colour = NA) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, 190)) +
  annotate("text", x = 14, y = 150, hjust = 0, size = 2.4,
           label = paste0("median ", fmt(median(d$permits_per_1000), 1),
                          "  mean ", fmt(mean(d$permits_per_1000), 1),
                          "\n", round(100 * mean(d$permits_per_1000 == 0)),
                          "% of towns at zero")) +
  labs(x = "Permits per 1,000 residents", y = "Towns",
       title = "(a) Permit rate")

q_hv <- d |>
  mutate(q = cut_number(log_hv, 5)) |>
  group_by(q) |>
  summarise(n = n(), med = median(permits_per_1000), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lab = paste0("Q", row_number()))

p_b <- q_hv |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lab, y = med)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey35", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(med, 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 2.3) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Home-value quintile", y = "Permits per 1,000",
       title = "(b) Housing wealth")

q_dens <- d |>
  mutate(q = cut_number(log_dens, 5)) |>
  group_by(q) |>
  summarise(n = n(), med = median(permits_per_1000), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lab = paste0("Q", row_number()))

p_c <- q_dens |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lab, y = med)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey35", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(med, 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 2.3) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Density quintile", y = "Permits per 1,000",
       title = "(c) Density")

p_a + p_b + p_c + plot_layout(widths = c(1.5, 1, 1)) &
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8.5))
```

Permit rates vary a lot from town to town. The median town issued
`r fmt(median(d$permits_per_1000), 1)` permits per 1,000 residents, but the upper
quartile is `r fmt(quantile(d$permits_per_1000, 0.75), 1)`, the maximum is
`r fmt(max(d$permits_per_1000), 0)`, and `r round(100 * mean(d$permits_per_1000 == 0))`%
of towns issued none at all. Panel (b) shows the first pattern we looked at: the
median rate climbs with housing wealth, from `r fmt(q_hv$med[1], 1)` permits per
1,000 in the cheapest quintile to `r fmt(q_hv$med[4], 1)` in the fourth, then drops
back a little. Panel (c) goes the other way, which surprised us. The sparsest
quintile has the highest rate (`r fmt(q_dens$med[1], 1)`), and the other four are
close to five.

```{r}
#| label: fig-geo
#| fig-cap: "Permit intensity by county. Bars are aggregate permits per 1,000 residents; the dashed line is the statewide rate. Counties are ordered by intensity."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.1
state_rate <- 1000 * n_permits / sum(d$census_population_24)

cty <- d |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(permits = sum(perm_total), pop = sum(census_population_24),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = 1000 * permits / pop)

cty |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(county, rate), y = rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey35", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = state_rate, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt(rate, 1)), hjust = -0.2, size = 2.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Permits per 1,000 residents")
```

Aggregate rates differ by a factor of six between counties, from
`r fmt(min(cty$rate), 1)` permits per 1,000 residents in
`r cty$county[which.min(cty$rate)]` to `r fmt(max(cty$rate), 1)` in
`r cty$county[which.max(cty$rate)]`. That ranking is not the one we would have
guessed. The top of the list is rural and inland, and the two most populous counties
sit in the middle, which is part of why county stays in the model as a control
rather than as a stand-in for size.

# Methods

Work was done in R with tidymodels; the preprocessing is in `R/data_prep.R` and the
models in `R/models.R`. The response is $\log(1 + \text{permits per 1,000
residents})$. Rates cannot be negative, they are skewed hard to the right, and
`r n_zero` towns issued nothing at all, so we add one before taking logs. On that
scale an RMSE of 0.8 is roughly a factor of $e^{0.8}$ in the raw rate, which is the
right way to read the tables below.

We fit each task as a ladder of models, holding the recipe and the resampling fixed
so that the comparison is fair:

- Size only: OLS of the rate on log population.
- Size plus county: the same model with 15 county dummies.
- Characteristics: the seven predictors, no county.
- Characteristics plus county: the full specification.
- Ridge and lasso: the same design, with the penalty tuned over 20 values.
- Random forest (`ranger`), tuning `mtry` and `min_n`.
- XGBoost, tuning depth, learning rate and `min_n`.

The second task repeats the ladder with a binary outcome, whether the town permitted
any multifamily unit at all, and scores models by AUC instead of RMSE.

We expected collinearity to be a problem and it was: population and density
correlate at 0.91, income and home value at 0.65, and variance inflation factors
reach 8.2 and 7.4. Ridge and lasso are in the ladder as a check on how much of the
county effect is genuine rather than an artifact of that overlap.

Every model is scored by repeated 10-fold cross-validation with three repetitions,
with folds stratified on the outcome for the multifamily task. Tuning happens inside
each resample, so the numbers reported are out of fold and no model has seen its own
test rows. Fits are cached in `results/*.rds`, so the report can be rebuilt without
refitting.

The tuning settled on small models: a ridge penalty of 0.0886, a lasso penalty of
0.0264, a forest with `mtry` 2 and `min_n` 2, and boosting at depth 2 with a
learning rate of 0.005.

# Results

## Permit rate

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reg
#| tbl-pos: "H"
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-validated performance for the permit-rate regression. The response is log(1 + permits per 1,000); standard errors are over the 30 resamples; the last column compares RMSE with the full OLS model."
tab <- reg$metrics |>
  select(model, .metric, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean) |>
  left_join(reg$metrics |> select(model, .metric, se = std_err) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = se),
            by = "model", suffix = c("", "_se")) |>
  mutate(rel = 100 * (rmse / rmse[model == "Characteristics + county (OLS)"] - 1)) |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `RMSE (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", rmse, rmse_se),
            `MAE (SE)`  = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", mae, mae_se),
            `R2 (SE)`   = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", rsq, rsq_se),
            `vs OLS` = if_else(abs(rel) < 0.05, "--", sprintf("%+.1f%%", rel)))
kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, align = "lrrrr", linesep = "")

```

Population on its own explains `r round(100 * get_reg("Size only (OLS)", "rsq"))`%
of the out-of-fold variance. Adding the seven characteristics takes that to
`r round(100 * get_reg("Characteristics (OLS)", "rsq"))`%, and adding the county
dummies as well reaches
`r round(100 * get_reg("Characteristics + county (OLS)", "rsq"))`%, so the
characteristics roughly double what population buys and county is worth another few
points on top.

The flexible models do not improve on this. The random forest has the best $R^2$
(`r fmt(get_reg("Random forest", "rsq"), 3)`), but its RMSE sits inside one standard
error of the OLS model, and XGBoost comes out slightly worse than OLS. Ridge
collapses back to OLS (the selected penalty is essentially zero) and lasso keeps
most of the county dummies at a small penalty, which says the county effects are not
an artifact of the dummy expansion. Our reading is that on the log scale the
relationship is close to additive, and a quarter of the variance is roughly the
ceiling for this feature set.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coef
#| tbl-cap: "Standardised OLS coefficients for the permit rate, per one standard deviation change in each predictor, with 95% intervals. County effects are omitted here but included in the fitted model."
coef_tab <- reg$std_coef |>
  filter(term %in% names(term_lab)) |>
  mutate(ord = match(term, names(term_lab)),
         Variable = term_lab[term],
         `Std. coef.` = sprintf("%+.3f", estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("%+.2f to %+.2f", estimate - 1.96 * std.error,
                            estimate + 1.96 * std.error),
         p = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001",
                     formatC(p.value, format = "f", digits = 3))) |>
  arrange(ord) |>
  select(Variable, `Std. coef.`, `95% CI`, `p value` = p)
kable(coef_tab, booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, align = "lrrr", linesep = "")

```

Home value is the main story. One standard deviation of median home value goes with
a `r fmt(abs(reg$std_coef$estimate[reg$std_coef$term == "log_hv"]), 2)` standard
deviation increase in the log permit rate, and in the unstandardised model a doubling
of home value corresponds to roughly a
`r fmt(exp(reg$ols_tidy$estimate[reg$ols_tidy$term == "log_hv"] * log(2)), 2)`-fold
higher rate. Income takes the wrong sign
(`r fmt(reg$std_coef$estimate[reg$std_coef$term == "log_inc"], 2)`) and cannot be
separated from zero once home value is in the model, so we do not read anything into
it. Population and density are both negative and are hard to pull apart; the plain
way to say it is that, conditional on county and on each other, larger and denser
towns permit less per resident. The multifamily share of the existing stock is
positive, which fits the obvious explanation that towns which already have
apartments keep building them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pdp
#| fig-cap: "Partial dependence of the permit rate on three predictors, from the OLS model (solid) and XGBoost (dashed). Each panel varies one predictor and holds the others at their observed values."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 1.8
lab_map <- c(log_hv = "log median home value", log_dens = "log population density",
             log_inc = "log median household income")

pdp_all <- bind_rows(reg$pdp, reg$pdp_ols) |>
  mutate(value = coalesce(log_hv, log_dens, log_inc),
         variable = factor(variable, levels = c("log_hv", "log_dens", "log_inc")))

ggplot(pdp_all, aes(x = value, y = pred, linetype = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x", labeller = as_labeller(lab_map)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted log(1 + rate)", linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 7))
```

Figure 3 is the same result from the other side. The XGBoost curves follow the
directions of the OLS slopes, but they flatten in the middle of the range and bend
at the ends, where there are fewer towns to learn from. Home value is the exception
and stays monotone over almost its whole range. Density is flat above about 100
residents per square mile and rises only among the emptiest towns.

We checked the fit two ways. The zeros were the first worry: refitting on the
`r n_towns - n_zero` towns with a strictly positive rate, using a plain
$\log(\text{rate})$ response, leaves the coefficients in the same direction and
about the same size (home value 0.72 against 0.99, population -0.39, density -0.24,
multifamily share 2.00), so the zero towns are not driving the result. The second is
the reporting channel, discussed above; keeping it in the model means the
coefficients are conditional on who counted the permits.

## Multifamily housing

The outcome here is binary, so the same predictors and the same resampling are
scored by AUC rather than RMSE.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-clf
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-validated performance for the multifamily classification (mf_any). Sensitivity and specificity are at the 0.5 threshold."
clf_tab <- clf$metrics |>
  select(model, .metric, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean) |>
  left_join(clf$metrics |> select(model, .metric, se = std_err) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = se),
            by = "model", suffix = c("", "_se")) |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `AUC (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", roc_auc, roc_auc_se),
            `Accuracy (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", accuracy, accuracy_se),
            Sensitivity = sprintf("%.2f", sens),
            Specificity = sprintf("%.2f", spec))
kable(clf_tab, booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, align = "lrrrr", linesep = "")

```

Telling apart towns that permitted multifamily housing is much easier than
explaining the rate; every model lands around AUC `r fmt(mean(m_clf$roc_auc), 2)`.
What interested us is that the characteristics add nothing. Logistic regression on
log population alone gets `r fmt(get_clf("Size only (logistic)", "roc_auc"), 3)`,
and the best of the four full models, `r clf$best_model`, gets
`r fmt(max(m_clf$roc_auc), 3)`, a difference well inside the noise. Whether a town
permits any apartments at all is mostly a question of how large it is.

# Discussion

Housing wealth, not household income, is what tracks where Maine builds. That is
the finding we would lead with, and it is not what we expected going in; income is
the variable everyone reaches for first. The two correlate at 0.65, so the pair is
best read together: what looks like a market signal is the value of what is already
there, not the earning power of the people who live there.

Density running negative is the second finding, and the one we trust least, because
population and density are nearly the same variable in a state with this settlement
pattern. We would not want to claim that denser towns build less; the safer claim is
that the emptiest fifth of towns builds at roughly double the median rate, which is
consistent with construction on cheap land at the edge of service centers.

The third finding is the ceiling. Even the forest, with every characteristic and 15
county dummies, explains about a quarter of the out-of-fold variance in the log
rate, and the flexible models do not beat the additive one. That tells us the
missing variables are not model capacity; they are zoning, sewer and water capacity,
buildable land, local politics and the age of the population, none of which the ACS
publishes at this geography. A quarter of the variance is a real result about how
much of local permitting is municipal socio-economics rather than a modeling
failure.

Two limitations we should flag. The sample drops the 90 towns that do not report,
and those are the smallest places, so what we describe is the permitting behavior
of towns that build and report rather than of the state as a whole; the 20-odd towns
with suppressed income or home value sit in the same corner of the sample. And this
is a single cross-section, so home value is as much an outcome of scarcity as a
cause of construction, and the coefficients are descriptive contrasts rather than
effects.

If we did this again we would start from the rate rather than the count, since we
spent a while modeling a target that turned out to be mostly population. The
obvious next step is a panel: the state has only a few years of annual reporting so
far, but once there are more, town fixed effects would absorb the local politics
that currently sit in the error term.
